summary.text: The Mariana Trench is the deepest oceanic trench on Earth, a crescent about 2,550 km long in the western Pacific, east of the Mariana Islands.
It forms where the old, cool, dense western edge of the Pacific plate is thrust beneath the smaller Mariana plate to the west.
Its deepest point, the Challenger Deep, is more than 2 km farther from sea level than the peak of Mount Everest.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: The Mariana Islands, named for Queen Mariana of Austria

items.prompt: The Mariana Islands next to the trench are volcanic. What sets off the melting beneath them?

options.label: Friction heat as the plates grind together
A hot plume rising from deep in the mantle
Water released from the sinking Pacific plate
Pressure from the trench's deep water

items.explain: Water trapped in minerals of the subducted Pacific plate is released and causes flux melting of the upper mantle.

items.prompt: Where the two plates meet, the western edge of the Pacific plate sits far lower than the neighbouring Mariana plate. Why?

options.label: Its old crust is cooler and denser
It is the smaller of the two plates
It is younger and still soft
It carries the heavier islands

items.explain: Crust at the Pacific plate's western edge is some of the oldest on Earth, cooler and denser, hence its great height difference from the younger Mariana plate.

items.prompt: Roughly how many times normal sea-level air pressure does the water press on the bottom of the trench?

options.label: About 10 times
About 100 times
About 100,000 times
About 1,000 times

items.explain: The water column exerts about 1,086 bar, approximately 1,071.8 times standard atmospheric pressure at sea level.

items.prompt: In 2009 the US made a national monument of the parts of the trench inside its exclusive economic zone. Why does it leave out the Challenger Deep?

options.label: It is too deep to patrol or protect
It lies in Micronesia's economic zone
It is reserved for military testing
It belongs to Japan by old treaty

items.explain: The monument covers only trench areas inside the US zone, and the Challenger Deep lies inside the zone of the Federated States of Micronesia.

items.prompt: In 1875 the trench's depth was found by lowering a weighted rope; in 1951 Challenger II used echo sounding instead. What did the change bring?

options.label: Pictures of the seafloor for the first time
Temperature readings along with depth
Far greater precision with much less effort
Depths taken without stopping the ship

items.explain: Echo sounding was a much more precise and vastly easier way to measure depth than the sounding equipment and drag lines of the first expedition.

items.prompt: Deep in the trench the water is near freezing and the pressure is crushing. What did researchers find living 10.6 km down?

options.label: Single-celled organisms
Nothing alive at all
Only giant squid
Only visiting whales

items.explain: Scripps researchers found single-celled organisms called monothalamea at a record depth of 10.6 km.

paragraphs.heading: The deepest trench
paragraphs.text: The Mariana Trench is the deepest ocean trench on Earth. It lies in the western Pacific about 200 km east of the Mariana Islands, and is a crescent about 2,550 km long and 69 km wide. Its deepest known point, 10,935 ± 6 m down, lies in the Challenger Deep, a small slot-shaped valley in its floor, at that valley's southern end. That spot is more than 2 km farther from sea level than the top of Mount Everest.

paragraphs.heading: Crushing and cold
paragraphs.text: At the bottom, the water overhead presses with 1,086 bar, roughly 1,071.8 times normal air pressure at sea level, or eight tons on every square inch. The water there is 1 to 4 °C. Life is still present: Scripps researchers found single-celled organisms called monothalamea 10.6 km down, a record depth. Data also suggest that microbes thrive in the trench.

paragraphs.heading: How it formed
paragraphs.text: Two tectonic plates meet here, along a boundary called the Izu–Bonin–Mariana subduction system. There the western edge of the Pacific plate is thrust under the smaller Mariana plate to its west, a process called subduction. That edge is some of the oldest ocean crust on Earth, up to 170 million years old, so it is cooler and denser, hence the great height difference with the younger Mariana plate. Water locked in minerals of the sinking Pacific plate is released, which melts the upper mantle and creates the volcanic Mariana Islands.

paragraphs.heading: Name and protection
paragraphs.text: The trench takes its name from the nearby Mariana Islands, which honor the Spanish queen Mariana of Austria under the name Las Marianas. The islands sit on the Mariana plate, on the western side of the trench. In 2009 the United States made the parts of the trench inside its exclusive economic zone into the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument. The Challenger Deep is left out, as it lies in the zone of the Federated States of Micronesia.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the depth
paragraphs.text: The Challenger expedition found the trench in 1875 by lowering a weighted rope, which recorded 8,184 m. In 1899 USS Nero measured 9,636 m. In 1951 Challenger II used echo sounding, far more precise and much easier than ropes, and recorded 10,900 m at the spot now called the Challenger Deep. In 1957 the Soviet ship Vityaz reported 11,034 m at a place it called the Mariana Hollow.

paragraphs.heading: Going to the bottom
paragraphs.text: By 2022 there had been 22 crewed and seven uncrewed descents. The first was the bathyscaphe Trieste, which carried Don Walsh and Jacques Piccard to the bottom on 23 January 1960, using gasoline for buoyancy and iron shot as ballast. Its instruments read 11,521 m, later revised to 10,916 m. The uncrewed vehicles Kaikō and Nereus followed in 1996 and 2009, and film director James Cameron made the fourth descent on 26 March 2012.
